name: Network decontamination

origin.note: Capture of an intruder by mobile agents (SPAA 2002).

related.relation: Both are security problems for agents in a hostile network: in black hole search the network destroys agents, in decontamination agents must clear a network that an arbitrarily fast intruder (or contamination) can re-enter.

summary: A team of agents must clean a contaminated network, or equivalently capture an invisible, arbitrarily fast intruder, using as few agents as possible.
statement: All nodes are initially **contaminated**. A node is **cleaned** when an agent visits it and is **recontaminated** when it has a contaminated neighbour and no agent **guards** it (stands on it). Agents move along edges from a **home base** $s$, the node where they all start; the clean part must stay connected. **Agents** is the number needed (the primary measure); **moves** (edge traversals) and time are secondary.

primer.intro: Imagine a network of pipes filled with a contaminating gas: cleaners must clean every junction, but gas flows back into any clean junction that is left unguarded next to one still full of gas. We model the network as a graph: junctions are **nodes**, pipes are **edges**, and each cleaner is an **agent**. At the start every node is **contaminated**. An agent makes a node **clean** by standing on it; a clean node with no agent on it becomes contaminated again as soon as one of its neighbours is contaminated (**recontamination**). An agent that stays on a clean node to prevent this is a **guard**. All agents start at one node $s$, the **home base**, and **move** along edges (one move is one traversal of one edge), and the clean part must always be connected. In the basic version the graph is a **tree** (a graph without cycles) whose map the agents know. The task: clean every node; we count the agents needed first, and moves and time second.

ideas.title: Guard the node, clean its branches one by one
ideas.idea:
A standard approach on a tree, rooted at the home base $s$. Write $a(v)$ for the number of agents this method uses to clean the **branch** of node $v$: $v$ together with all nodes below it.

1. A node with no children (a **leaf**) needs one agent: $a(v) = 1$.
2. At a node $v$, sort the branches of its children so that the first one needs the most agents.
3. Keep one agent on $v$ as a guard. Clean the other branches one after another, each with its own team; when a branch is clean, its team comes back to $v$ to clean the next one.
4. Finally the guard is no longer needed at $v$ (all its other neighbours are clean), so it joins the team for the first, largest branch.
5. This gives $a(v) = \max\big(a(c_1),\ a(c_2) + 1\big)$, where $c_1$ and $c_2$ are the children with the largest and second-largest needs.
ideas.analysis: No clean node is ever left unguarded next to a contaminated one, so nothing gets recontaminated, and the clean part always contains $s$ and stays connected. A path needs one agent; a star centred at $s$ needs two; a complete binary tree of height $h$ needs $h + 1$ with this rule, so about $\log n$ agents for $n$ nodes. [Barriere2002Capture] compute the smallest possible team for any tree, and a strategy for it, in linear time; this primer does not claim that the simple rule above always matches it.
ideas.why_it_matters: The idea of a guard that waits at a node until its last branch is clean underlies decontamination strategies on trees and on many structured networks.

ideas.title: One agent cannot clean a cycle
ideas.idea: A standard argument. Let the graph be a ring and let one agent start at $s$. As soon as the agent steps to a neighbour, $s$ is unguarded, and its other neighbour is still contaminated, so $s$ becomes contaminated again. The agent can never have more than its current node clean.
ideas.analysis: So any graph containing a cycle needs at least two agents: one guards while the other advances. More generally, the team must be large enough to guard every clean node that touches a contaminated node at every moment, which is why the answer depends on the shape of the graph (for the hypercube, $\Theta(n/\sqrt{\log n})$ agents for $n$ nodes [Flocchini2008Hypercubes]).
ideas.why_it_matters: It shows the basic counting idea of the problem: count the boundary between clean and contaminated parts that must be guarded.

ideas.title: The adversary grows the tree as you clean it
ideas.idea: Now the agents do not know the graph, and they must never let a clean part become contaminated again (the strategy is **monotone**). An **adversary** (an imagined opponent) builds the graph while the agents clean it [Ilcinkas2009Monotonicity]. Whenever an agent crosses an edge into the unknown, the adversary attaches at the far end a new node with two more unexplored edges. Every clean node that still has an unexplored edge must be guarded, because the edge may lead to contamination. When the graph has reached $n$ nodes, the adversary stops adding edges: the result is a tree in which each node has at most three edges.
ideas.analysis: At the end, every parent of a leaf in this tree has had to be guarded, and there are at least about $n/4$ such nodes, so the protocol used at least about $n/4$ agents. A team that knew the tree in advance could clean it with only $O(\log n)$ agents. So not knowing the graph costs a factor $\Omega(n/\log n)$ in team size, and [Ilcinkas2009Monotonicity] give an algorithm that achieves this factor, even for asynchronous agents.
ideas.why_it_matters: It is a clean example of a *competitive* lower bound: comparing a distributed team without a map to the best team with a map.

history: From the start the objective was the **minimum number of agents** [Barriere2002Capture], first on special topologies [Flocchini2008Hypercubes] and then on unknown graphs, where the question becomes the competitive ratio against the optimal team [Ilcinkas2009Monotonicity]. Monotone strategies in dynamic graphs, whose edges may disappear, were studied by [Bar2026Monotone].

axes.name: Knowledge

values.label: the topology is known
values.definition: The topology is known to the agents (or to a coordinator).

axes.origin: Barrière, Flocchini, Fraigniaud and Santoro introduced contiguous search by mobile agents, in which agents cannot jump and the cleared part must stay connected; they solved it on trees with a linear-time algorithm that computes the minimum team and its strategy, and stressed that the algorithm is naturally distributed, so a tree network can compute its own strategy [Barriere2002Capture] (abstract read). Later work on specific topologies also builds the strategy from the known structure; for hypercubes, Flocchini, Huang and Luccio use a coordinator that leads the other agents [Flocchini2008Hypercubes]. The unknown level asks what is lost when searchers must clear a graph they discover as they go. Blin, Fraigniaud, Nisse and Vial cleared any unknown asynchronous anonymous graph with whiteboards using at most one searcher more than the monotone connected search number from the homebase, each searcher with $O(\log k)$ bits of memory (Theorem 1); the clearing is connected but not necessarily monotone, and the number of moves may be exponential [Blin2008Chasing]; Ilcinkas, Nisse and Soguet showed that if clearing must also be monotone, a protocol with no a priori information about the graph has competitive ratio $\Theta(n/\log n)$ in the number of searchers, the lower bound holding even for synchronous searchers on trees of maximum degree 3 [Ilcinkas2009Monotonicity].

variants.title: Trees
variants.summary: On trees the minimum team and a strategy are computed in linear time.

results.note: Introductory and current best; also a decentralised version with a linear number of messages.

variants.title: Hypercubes
variants.summary: A hypercube needs $\Theta(n/\sqrt{\log n})$ agents, matching its pathwidth.

results.note: Introductory and current best (with a coordinator); with visibility, $n/2$ agents in $O(\log n)$ time.

variants.title: Unknown graphs, monotone strategies
variants.summary: Clearing an unknown graph monotonically costs a factor $\Theta(n/\log n)$ in agents over the optimum.

variants.title: Dynamic graphs, monotone strategies
variants.summary: In a 1-interval connected dynamic graph whose edges may stay missing indefinitely, $D+2(m-n+1)$ co-located synchronous agents clean an unknown graph monotonically, $m-n+1$ being its cyclomatic number; on wheels $n$ agents are needed.
variants.statement: The graph is the footprint $G$ (with $n$ nodes, $m$ edges and diameter $D$) of a dynamic graph that is connected in every round: the adversary may remove any edges as long as the graph stays connected, and a missing edge may stay missing for ever. $m-n+1$ is the cyclomatic number of $G$, the number of edges outside a spanning tree. Nodes **and edges** start contaminated: an agent cleans a node by visiting it and an edge by crossing it, and a clean node or edge becomes contaminated again when a path without agents joins it to a contaminated node or edge. The strategy must be **monotone**. Agents start at a home base $s$ chosen by the adversary, are synchronous, have distinct identifiers, communicate only at the same node, and know nothing about $G$; at a node they see which incident edges are present and which are contaminated.

preconditions: holds even when every missing edge reappears within a bounded time
Theorem 2 and Corollary 1: $m-n+1$ co-located agents fail on a wheel with $n-1$ rim nodes, where $m-n+1 = n-1$, starting at the hub
the adversary keeps every rim edge missing until each rim node is guarded, then restores them all
needs edges that may stay missing indefinitely

assumes: agents see which incident edges are present and which are contaminated
results.note: Introductory and current best (Theorem 5; time from Lemma 6). Every node becomes clean; an edge that never reappears cannot be cleaned (Remark 5).

assumes: every missing edge reappears within $\delta$ rounds
every missing edge reappears within $\delta$ rounds
results.note: Theorem 3: agents settle on the nodes in breadth-first order and one agent then cleans the remaining edges; fewer agents than $D+m-n+1$ on dense graphs.

agents.note: $D+2(m-n+1)$ agents, which is $\Theta(n^2)$ on dense graphs, against $n-1$ on $K_{n/2,n/2}$ and $m-n+2 = n$ on wheels; Bar et al. state that their bounds are not tight.

open: How many co-located agents are necessary and sufficient to clean every 1-interval connected dynamic graph monotonically, as a function of $n$, $m$ and $D$? $D+2(m-n+1)$ suffice, and $n-1$ (on $K_{n/2,n/2}$) and $n$ (on wheels) can be necessary [Bar2026Monotone].
variants.notes: Checked against the full text of [Bar2026Monotone] (arXiv v1; the cited CALDAM 2026 version was not read). Bar, Barik, Bhattacharya and Mandal call this model of dynamics *indefinite edge disappearance*; in their *finite time edge reappearance* model every missing edge reappears within $\delta$ rounds (their $T$ is $\delta$ here, their $k$ is $m-n+1$ and their $d$ is $D$). It is a special case, so its lower bounds hold here. The algorithm of Theorem 5 keeps one agent at each node with a missing incident edge until the edge reappears, and one more agent at a node with two or more visible contaminated edges, while the rest of the team continues a depth-first search. Lemma 1 states that on some graph of diameter $D$ fewer than $D$ co-located agents fail, in both models; it is not recorded as a bound here, because its proof (on a complete binary tree, Fig. 3) could not be confirmed.

figure.caption: Decontamination of a tree [Barriere2002Capture] with the rule "guard the node, clean its branches one by one": every node is contaminated (red) and agents start at the home base $s$; a node is clean (green) once visited and would be recontaminated if left unguarded next to a red node. One agent guards $s$ while the other cleans the smaller branch and comes back; then the guard is free, both enter the other branch, and the same rule is applied at $a$. Nothing is ever recontaminated, the clean part stays connected, and two agents suffice.

frames.label: Start: all nodes contaminated; agents 1, 2 at s
Agent 1 guards s; agent 2 cleans the smaller branch b
Branch b is clean: the guard at s is no longer needed
Both enter branch a; agent 1 guards a, agent 2 cleans a2
Last branch: the guard joins; every node is clean with 2 agents

further.note: Cops and a lethal robber on a ring: synchronous agents (cops) with distinct identifiers and $O(\log n)$ bits, placed at arbitrary nodes and knowing nothing about the ring, face an invisible robber that knows their algorithm, moves arbitrarily fast along paths without agents between the agents' moves, may not enter a node with an agent, and destroys every agent that enters its node; the agents win when they occupy both neighbours of the robber. $n$ agents never suffice, even when they start at one node (Theorem 2.1), and $\max\{\sigma+\lfloor\log\sigma\rfloor+4,\ n-\sigma+4\}$ agents win within $O(n^3)$ rounds, where $\sigma$ is the length of the part of the ring between the nearest agents that initially contains the robber (Theorem 4.1; their $\rho$ is $\sigma$ here); from a single starting node this is $n+\lfloor\log n\rfloor+4$ (Remark 4.1). The robber is an arbitrarily fast intruder that also destroys agents, so the problem combines intruder capture with black hole search. Preprint; read.

Black virus decontamination of synchronous rings by initially scattered agents: a contaminated node that, when visited, destroys the agent and infects its unguarded neighbours. Abstract of the SIROCCO 2020 version read.
Decontamination with temporal immunity: the immunity number, the least time a clean node can stay exposed to a contaminated neighbour, for one agent on several graph classes. Abstract read.

Decontamination with immunity: a clean node left without an agent is recontaminated only when at least a threshold number of its neighbours are contaminated (the usual model has threshold 1). For $d$-dimensional meshes, tori and trees, monotone algorithms whose team shrinks as the threshold grows (on a mesh one agent once the threshold reaches $d$, Theorem 1), lower bounds on the team that match for some thresholds (Theorems 2, 4, 5), and $\Theta(n)$ moves, which is optimal. The agents are synchronous; with one more agent the algorithms work asynchronously. Read (model and theorems).

Decontamination of butterfly networks with an immunity threshold, judged by work: the number of agents times the number of parallel steps, at least $n$. For some thresholds a protocol with a larger team needs less work than the protocol with the smallest team known; optimality is shown only in simple cases, and lower bounds on agents and steps are left open. Read (model, protocols and costs).

A continuous relative: one agent inside a simple polygon must detect an intruder that moves arbitrarily fast. An agent with two flashlights can search every polygon that an agent with a light in all directions can, as conjectured in 1992 and proved by Park et al. in 2001; a simpler proof through a 2-link visibility diagram of the polygon (Theorems 1–3). Read (statements and outline).
